spots.name: Ada Lovelace's St James's Square Home
spots.subject: Ada Lovelace (1815–1852), mathematician and pioneer of computing
spots.whyGo: Lovelace's notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine are considered the first published algorithm intended for a machine - a real claim to "first computer programmer".
spots.opNote: A private/institutional building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Agatha Christie's Home
spots.subject: Agatha Christie (1890–1976), novelist and playwright
spots.whyGo: Christie lived here while writing some of her best-known Poirot and Marple novels - a quiet Holland Park backstreet a world away from the murders on the page.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Alan Turing's Birthplace
spots.subject: Alan Turing (1912–1954), mathematician and codebreaker
spots.whyGo: Turing was born here - the father of theoretical computer science and the codebreaker whose work at Bletchley Park is credited with shortening the Second World War.
spots.opNote: A private residential building (now a hotel) - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Alexander Fleming's Chelsea Home
spots.subject: Alexander Fleming (1881–1955), discoverer of penicillin
spots.whyGo: Fleming's discovery of penicillin is one of the most consequential moments in modern medicine - his home plaque sits a short walk from where he worked at St Mary's.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Alfred Hitchcock's South Kensington Home
spots.subject: Alfred Hitchcock (1899–1980), film director
spots.whyGo: Hitchcock lived here before his move to Hollywood - a plaque for one of cinema's defining directors on one of South Kensington's busiest roads.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building on a main road - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Banksy's "Despair Ends, Tactics Begin"
spots.subject: A 2019 piece near Marble Arch
spots.whyGo: Appeared in April 2019 near Marble Arch, at the junction of Oxford Street and Park Lane - one of the older pieces on this list to have survived this long in place.
spots.opNote: Street-level, out in the open at a very high-footfall junction.

spots.name: Banksy's "His Master's Voice"
spots.subject: A 2003 piece, one of the oldest survivors in the former Cargo courtyard
spots.whyGo: One of the oldest pieces on this list, dating to 2003 - a dog listening to a gramophone-style speaker, a play on the old HMV logo.
spots.opNote: Street-level in the same courtyard as Guard Dog - visit them together.

spots.name: Banksy's "TV Out Window"
spots.subject: The second preserved 2004 piece at the Art'otel London Hoxton
spots.whyGo: The second of the two pieces the Art'otel was built around - a figure throwing a television out of a window, preserved on the same building as the Knife-and-Fork Rat.
spots.opNote: Structurally preserved as part of the hotel building - visit alongside the Knife-and-Fork Rat.

spots.name: Banksy's Basquiat "Stop and Search"
spots.subject: The second 2017 Basquiat tribute piece in the same tunnel
spots.whyGo: The second of the pair of 2017 Basquiat-tribute pieces in the same tunnel - a police officer frisking a crowned Basquiat-style figure, a pointed comment on how the artist himself was treated by police in life.
spots.opNote: Inside the same protected road tunnel as the Ferris Wheel piece - visit both together.

spots.name: Banksy's Basquiat Ferris Wheel
spots.subject: One of two 2017 Basquiat tribute pieces in the Beech Street tunnel
spots.whyGo: Painted in 2017 to coincide with a Basquiat exhibition at the Barbican, reworking Basquiat's crown motif - among the best-preserved Banksy pieces in London precisely because it was protected not long after it appeared.
spots.opNote: Inside a road tunnel, protected - one of the more reliably-still-there pieces on this list.

spots.name: Banksy's Cannon Street Rat
spots.subject: An early-2000s rat stencil on a railway bridge
spots.whyGo: One of Banksy's earliest surviving London rats, on the railway bridge over Cannon Street - a reminder of how much of his early-2000s stencil work has simply vanished since, making survivors like this one worth seeking out.
spots.opNote: On a railway bridge structure, viewable from the street.

spots.name: Banksy's Elephants
spots.subject: Two elephant heads reaching toward each other from blocked windows
spots.whyGo: Two elephant heads stencilled reaching toward one another from a pair of bricked-up windows - one of the more visually striking and best-preserved pieces still on a public street.
spots.opNote: Street-level, out in the open on a residential corner.

spots.name: Banksy's Fishing Boy
spots.subject: A 2008 piece on the Thames Path at Bermondsey Wall
spots.whyGo: A 2008 piece right on the Thames Path, showing a boy fishing - part of a small cluster of riverside Banksy pieces along this stretch of the south bank.
spots.opNote: Outdoors on the riverside path, exposed to weather - one to see while it lasts.

spots.name: Banksy's Flag-Blinded Statue
spots.subject: A bronze-effect figure stepping off its plinth, face obscured by a flag - confirmed by Banksy in April 2026
spots.whyGo: Appeared overnight in April 2026 and was confirmed as Banksy's own within a day - a suited figure stepping off its plinth with its face wrapped in a flag, widely read as a comment on blind patriotism. The newest and most-visited piece on this list.
spots.opNote: Out in the open on a public street - drew huge crowds on arrival and its long-term fate (left in place, protected, or removed) was still unclear as of this write-up. Check it's still there before making a special trip.

spots.name: Banksy's Graffiti Painter (after Velázquez)
spots.subject: A 2008 piece riffing on Velázquez, on Portobello Road
spots.whyGo: A 2008 piece at the junction of Acklam Road and Portobello Road, riffing on a Velázquez composition with a figure caught mid-graffiti - one of the better-known survivors from Banksy's most prolific Notting Hill years.
spots.opNote: Street-level on a well-known corner - worth combining with a Portobello Market visit.

spots.name: Banksy's Guard Dog
spots.subject: A 2013 piece in the former Cargo courtyard, Shoreditch
spots.whyGo: One of several Banksy pieces clustered around the former Cargo nightclub's courtyard on Rivington Street - Shoreditch's Banksy density rivals anywhere else in London.
spots.opNote: Street-level in a courtyard off Rivington Street. Combine with the other Cargo-courtyard and Art'otel pieces nearby.

spots.name: Banksy's Knife-and-Fork Rat
spots.subject: A 2004 rat piece, now part of the Art'otel London Hoxton
spots.whyGo: The Art'otel London Hoxton was built to deliberately preserve two Banksy pieces on its site - a rat setting a table with a knife and fork - rather than paint over them, which is why both have survived so cleanly.
spots.opNote: Structurally preserved as part of the hotel building - among the most reliably-still-there pieces on this whole list.

spots.name: Banksy's Pink Car
spots.subject: An early-2000s piece at the Old Truman Brewery, Brick Lane
spots.whyGo: One of the early-2000s survivors at the Old Truman Brewery, right on Brick Lane - easy to combine with the market, the vintage shops and the curry houses on the same street.
spots.opNote: On the Truman Brewery site, street-visible.

spots.name: Banksy's Rat, The Standard Hotel
spots.subject: An early-2000s rat holding a placard, on the side of The Standard hotel
spots.whyGo: A classic rat-with-placard stencil on the side of The Standard hotel, a short walk from King's Cross and St Pancras stations - one of the most convenient pieces on this list for anyone arriving by train.
spots.opNote: On the exterior of the hotel building, street-visible at any time.

spots.name: Banksy's Royal Courts Protester
spots.subject: A stencil on the Royal Courts of Justice, appeared September 2025
spots.whyGo: A protest-themed stencil that appeared on the wall of the Royal Courts of Justice itself - a piece commenting on protest law, placed on one of the most symbolically loaded buildings Banksy could have picked.
spots.opNote: On a government building's exterior wall - visibility and preservation status can change fast on pieces like this. Check before visiting.

spots.name: Banksy's Stargazing Children, Bayswater
spots.subject: The second "Stargazing Children" piece, appeared December 2025
spots.whyGo: The Bayswater half of a pair of related pieces that appeared within months of each other in 2025 - worth knowing about even if you only make it to one.
spots.opNote: On a residential mews. Confirm it's still there before visiting - very recent pieces are the least predictable.

spots.name: Banksy's Stargazing Children, Centre Point
spots.subject: A 2025 piece near St Giles Square / Centre Point
spots.address: St Giles Square, near Centre Point
spots.whyGo: One of two "Stargazing Children" pieces that appeared in 2025 - this one near the foot of Centre Point, at the northern tip of Soho where it meets St Giles.
spots.opNote: Street-level, out in the open. As with all recent Banksy pieces, confirm it's still there before a special trip.

spots.name: Banksy/Robbo's "I Love London" Rat
spots.subject: A 2004 Banksy rat, later altered by rival artist King Robbo - a physical record of their feud
spots.whyGo: Started life in 2004 as a Banksy rat holding a placard reading "London Doesn't Work". Rival graffiti artist King Robbo later reworked the placard with his own tag and a heart, as one move in a years-long "graffiti war" between the two - the surviving piece is a genuine joint artefact, not a misattribution, and Banksy repainted a memorial version after Robbo was hospitalised.
spots.opNote: Street-level, out in the open - one of the older survivors, so check current condition before a special trip.

spots.name: Battersea Flower Station
spots.subject: A flower shop that opens into a long, hidden garden-centre corridor
spots.whyGo: Looks like an ordinary flower shop from the street; walk through and it opens into a long outdoor corridor of plants, bunting and fairy lights - a garden centre that was shut off to the public for 30 years before reopening. A second entrance exists on Winders Road.
spots.opNote: Free to browse, normal shop hours. A genuinely photogenic detour rather than a destination in itself.

spots.name: Bob Marley's Chelsea Flat
spots.subject: Bob Marley (1945–1981), singer and songwriter
spots.whyGo: One of English Heritage's more recent plaques (2019) and a rare popular-music honouree on a street otherwise dense with 19th-century names.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Cecil Court
spots.subject: An antiquarian bookshop alley, reputedly one inspiration for Diagon Alley
spots.whyGo: A pedestrian alley between Charing Cross Road and St Martin's Lane lined almost entirely with independent antiquarian and specialist bookshops - rare first editions, maps, theatre memorabilia. Its narrow shopfronts and Victorian character are often cited as a real-world echo of Diagon Alley.
spots.opNote: A public street, shops keep normal daytime hours and are closed Sundays for the most part - check individual shops.

spots.name: Cecil Day-Lewis's Greenwich Home
spots.subject: Cecil Day-Lewis (1904–1972), Poet Laureate
spots.whyGo: Day-Lewis lived here as Poet Laureate - Crooms Hill is one of Greenwich's prettiest streets, running alongside the park.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Charles Darwin at UCL
spots.subject: Charles Darwin (1809–1882), naturalist
spots.address: Biological Sciences Building, University College London, Gower Street
spots.whyGo: Marks Darwin's connection to UCL rather than a home address - a rare institutional plaque for the author of On the Origin of Species.
spots.opNote: On a university building - viewable from the street, campus generally open to walk through in daytime.

spots.name: Charles Dickens's Bloomsbury Home
spots.subject: Charles Dickens (1812–1870), novelist
spots.whyGo: Dickens wrote Oliver Twist and Nicholas Nickleby here - the only one of his London homes still standing, now the Charles Dickens Museum.
spots.opNote: Now the Charles Dickens Museum - a paid museum with set opening hours, not just a street plaque.

spots.name: Chopin's Last London Address
spots.subject: Frédéric Chopin (1810–1849), composer
spots.whyGo: Chopin stayed here during his final visit to London in 1848, a year before his death - a quiet corner of St James's with an outsized musical footnote.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Cloth Fair & St Bartholomew the Great
spots.subject: London's oldest parish church (1123) on one of its oldest surviving streets
spots.whyGo: St Bartholomew the Great was founded in 1123 and is the City's oldest parish church, with a Norman interior used in dozens of films. Cloth Fair, right beside it, has some of the only houses in the City to survive the 1666 Great Fire.
spots.opNote: The church charges a small entry fee for visitors (free for worship); Cloth Fair itself is a public street, walkable any time.

spots.name: Coleridge's Fitzrovia Home
spots.subject: Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834), poet
spots.whyGo: One of several London addresses for Coleridge, who wrote The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan - a quieter corner of Fitzrovia's literary map.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Devonshire Mews West
spots.subject: A quiet, ivy-clad Marylebone mews, essentially tourist-free
spots.whyGo: One of Marylebone's best-kept mews streets - cobbles, climbing ivy, converted coach houses - a couple of minutes off the high street but with almost none of its foot traffic.
spots.opNote: A private residential street; walkable and photographable, but treat it as someone's front door, not an attraction.

spots.name: Disraeli's Last Home
spots.subject: Benjamin Disraeli (1804–1881), Prime Minister
spots.whyGo: Disraeli died here in 1881, having twice served as Prime Minister - one of several PM plaques within a short walk of each other in Mayfair.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Home
spots.subject: Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1806–1861), poet
spots.whyGo: Browning lived here before her secret marriage to Robert Browning and elopement to Italy - the house her father is said to have locked her into is a short walk from Marylebone High Street.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Elizabeth Garrett Anderson's Home
spots.subject: Elizabeth Garrett Anderson (1836–1917), first woman to qualify as a doctor in Britain
spots.whyGo: Garrett Anderson forced open the medical profession to women in Britain, later founding what became the New Hospital for Women - a plaque marking a genuine first.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Florence Nightingale's Mayfair Home
spots.subject: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910), founder of modern nursing
spots.whyGo: Nightingale lived here for the last decades of her life, having already reformed nursing practice after the Crimean War.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Francis Bacon's Studio
spots.subject: Francis Bacon (1909–1992), painter
spots.whyGo: Bacon's studio here - famously chaotic, now reconstructed in Dublin's Hugh Lane Gallery - is where he painted for the last three decades of his life.
spots.opNote: A private mews building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Friedrich Engels's Primrose Hill Home
spots.subject: Friedrich Engels (1820–1895), philosopher and political theorist
spots.whyGo: Engels lived here for over 20 years, hosting Karl Marx regularly - a plaque for one half of one of history's most consequential intellectual partnerships.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: George Eliot's Last Home
spots.subject: George Eliot (1819–1880), novelist (Mary Ann Evans)
spots.whyGo: Eliot died here weeks after moving in - one of several literary plaques along Cheyne Walk's riverside stretch.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: George Orwell's Kentish Town Home
spots.subject: George Orwell (1903–1950), writer
spots.whyGo: One of several Orwell addresses across London - Kentish Town's plaque marks a working writer's home rather than a grand literary residence.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Gladstone's Home
spots.subject: William Ewart Gladstone (1809–1898), Prime Minister
spots.whyGo: One of the grandest addresses on the plaque map - Carlton House Terrace overlooks The Mall, a short walk from Westminster's core sights.
spots.opNote: A private/institutional building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Gracie Fields's Islington Home
spots.subject: Dame Gracie Fields (1898–1979), singer and entertainer
spots.whyGo: One of the biggest British entertainers of the 1930s, on Islington's main shopping street - a plaque worth combining with an Upper Street stop anyway.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building on a busy shopping street.

spots.name: Handel's House
spots.subject: George Frideric Handel (1685–1759), composer
spots.whyGo: Handel lived and composed here for 36 years, including Messiah. The house is now Handel & Hendrix House, a museum with two eras under one roof.
spots.opNote: The house is a paid museum, not just a plaque - the interesting bit is that Jimi Hendrix lived next door two centuries later.

spots.name: Henry James's Kensington Home
spots.subject: Henry James (1843–1916), writer
spots.whyGo: James wrote several of his major novels while living on this street - part of a dense cluster of literary Kensington plaques worth combining on one walk.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Ian Fleming's Belgravia Home
spots.subject: Ian Fleming (1908–1964), creator of James Bond
spots.whyGo: Fleming was born and grew up on this street - the plaque marks the creator of James Bond, a very different kind of London export from the writers nearby.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: J.M. Barrie's Bayswater Home
spots.subject: J.M. Barrie (1860–1937), creator of Peter Pan
spots.whyGo: Barrie lived facing Kensington Gardens, where Peter Pan is set and where his own statue of the character still stands - the plaque and the statue make a short, natural pairing.
spots.opNote: A private residential building facing the park - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: James Joyce's Kensington Home
spots.subject: James Joyce (1882–1941), author
spots.whyGo: One of the less-expected London addresses for Joyce, better known for Dublin and Trieste - the plaque marks a brief but real London chapter.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Jim Henson's Hampstead Home
spots.subject: Jim Henson (1936–1990), creator of the Muppets
spots.whyGo: One of English Heritage's newest plaques (2021) - a genuinely unexpected name to find on a Hampstead street among the poets and psychoanalysts.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Jimi Hendrix's Flat
spots.subject: Jimi Hendrix (1942–1970), musician
spots.whyGo: Hendrix lived here 1968-69, next door to where Handel lived 200 years earlier - the two plaques sit a few feet apart on the same street.
spots.opNote: Combined with Handel's House as Handel & Hendrix House, a paid museum covering both.

spots.name: John Lennon's Flat
spots.subject: John Lennon (1940–1980), musician
spots.whyGo: Lennon and Yoko Ono lived here - Ono herself unveiled the plaque, a rare case of the commemorated person's own partner doing the honours.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: John Maynard Keynes's Bloomsbury Home
spots.subject: John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946), economist
spots.whyGo: Keynes was part of the Bloomsbury Group centred on Gordon Square - his economic theory reshaped 20th-century policy far beyond the square itself.
spots.opNote: A private/institutional building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Joseph Conrad's Victoria Home
spots.subject: Joseph Conrad (1857–1924), novelist
spots.whyGo: Conrad lived here in the 1890s while working as a merchant seaman, before Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim - a short walk from Victoria station.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Joseph Grimaldi's Islington Home
spots.subject: Joseph Grimaldi (1778–1837), the original "Joey" clown
spots.whyGo: Grimaldi essentially invented the modern circus/pantomime clown - British clowns are still nicknamed "Joey" after him, and his grave nearby is a small park named for him.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Karl Marx's Soho Home
spots.subject: Karl Marx (1818–1883), philosopher and economist
spots.whyGo: Marx lived here in poverty with his family while writing much of Das Kapital - a few doors from where he and Engels regularly met.
spots.opNote: Above what is now a restaurant - the plaque is at first-floor level.

spots.name: Keats House
spots.subject: John Keats (1795–1821), Romantic poet
spots.whyGo: The oldest-issued plaque of this batch (1896) - Keats wrote Ode to a Nightingale reputedly under a plum tree in this garden. Now a small paid museum.
spots.opNote: Keats House is a paid museum with set opening hours, not just a street plaque.

spots.name: Kynance Mews
spots.subject: A wisteria-clad cobbled mews, a village pocket inside South Kensington
spots.whyGo: Converted stables on a cobbled cul-de-sac, walls thick with wisteria in late spring - the closest South Kensington gets to a country village lane, a few minutes from the museums.
spots.opNote: A private residential street; walkable and photographable, but treat it as someone's front door, not an attraction. Wisteria peaks late April to May.

spots.name: Lord Tennyson's Belgravia Home
spots.subject: Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892), Poet Laureate
spots.whyGo: Tennyson stayed here during his decades as Poet Laureate - The Charge of the Light Brigade and In Memoriam both date from his career.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Margot Fonteyn's Home
spots.subject: Margot Fonteyn (1919–1991), prima ballerina
spots.whyGo: Fonteyn danced at the Royal Opera House a short walk from here for decades - a plaque for one of British ballet's defining names, in the neighbourhood she performed in.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Mark Twain's Chelsea Home
spots.subject: Mark Twain (Samuel Langhorne Clemens, 1835–1910), writer
spots.whyGo: Twain lived here during one of his London periods, by then already the author of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Mary Seacole's Soho Home
spots.subject: Mary Seacole (1805–1881), Crimean War nurse and businesswoman
spots.whyGo: Seacole's plaque was re-erected here in 2007, marking where research showed she lived in 1857 after returning from nursing British soldiers in Crimea.
spots.opNote: On a building overlooking the square itself.

spots.name: Mary Shelley's Belgravia Home
spots.subject: Mary Shelley (1797–1851), author of Frankenstein
spots.whyGo: Shelley spent her last years here, decades after writing Frankenstein at 18 - a very different London chapter from the Gothic summer that made her famous.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Michael Faraday's Birthplace Area
spots.subject: Michael Faraday (1791–1867), scientist
spots.whyGo: Faraday's work on electromagnetism underpins the electric motor and generator - a genuinely foundational scientist commemorated on a quiet Marylebone street.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Mozart's Belgravia Home
spots.subject: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791), composer
spots.whyGo: Mozart composed his first symphony here in 1764, aged eight, during his family's 15-month stay in London.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Nancy Astor's Home
spots.subject: Nancy Astor (1879–1964), first woman to take a seat as an MP
spots.whyGo: Astor was the first woman to sit in the House of Commons - the plaque sits in the same St James's Square as several other notable addresses.
spots.opNote: A private/institutional building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Oscar Wilde's Chelsea Home
spots.subject: Oscar Wilde (1854–1900), writer and wit
spots.whyGo: Wilde lived here with his wife Constance while writing The Picture of Dorian Gray and his best-known plays, before his 1895 trials and imprisonment.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: P.G. Wodehouse's Mayfair Home
spots.subject: P.G. Wodehouse (1881–1975), writer, creator of Jeeves and Wooster
spots.whyGo: Wodehouse lived here before the Jeeves and Wooster novels made him one of the most quoted comic writers in English.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Peace Pagoda, Battersea Park
spots.subject: A 1985 Buddhist peace pagoda gifted to London, on the Thames path
spots.whyGo: Built by Buddhist monks and nuns of the Nipponzan Myohoji order and unveiled in 1985, this gilded pagoda sits right on the river inside Battersea Park - a striking landmark most people walking or cycling the Thames path have never actually stopped for.
spots.opNote: Free, always accessible within the park's opening hours. Best approached along the riverside path.

spots.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley's Soho Home
spots.subject: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822), Romantic poet
spots.whyGo: Shelley lodged here as a young radical, years before Ozymandias - a Soho address for one of Romantic poetry's biggest names.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Richard Burton's Hampstead Home
spots.subject: Richard Burton (1925–1984), actor
spots.whyGo: A relatively recent plaque (2011) for one of the best-known screen and stage actors of the 20th century.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Rosalind Franklin's Home
spots.subject: Rosalind Franklin (1920–1958), X-ray crystallographer, DNA structure pioneer
spots.whyGo: Franklin's X-ray diffraction images were essential to identifying the structure of DNA - a scientist whose contribution went under-credited for decades.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Rudolf Nureyev's Kensington Home
spots.subject: Rudolf Nureyev (1938–1993), ballet dancer
spots.whyGo: Nureyev's 1961 defection from the Soviet Union made global headlines - his London home plaque sits in one of Kensington's quieter residential streets.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Samuel Beckett's Chelsea Home
spots.subject: Samuel Beckett (1906–1989), playwright and novelist
spots.whyGo: Beckett lived here before Waiting for Godot - a Nobel laureate's London address shared with Patrick Blackett, another plaque at the same number.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Samuel Johnson's Covent Garden Base
spots.subject: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784), writer and lexicographer
spots.whyGo: Johnson compiled his Dictionary of the English Language while based in this part of London - Russell Street sits right by the piazza.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Samuel Pepys's Buckingham Street Homes
spots.subject: Samuel Pepys (1633–1703), diarist
spots.whyGo: Two separate plaques on the same short street mark two different Pepys residences - he seems to turn up everywhere in central London's plaque map.
spots.opNote: Two plaques, two buildings, a few doors apart - worth doing both on the same stop.

spots.name: Shad Thames
spots.subject: A cobbled Victorian warehouse street once nicknamed "the larder of London"
spots.whyGo: These 1873 warehouses stored the grain, spices and tea that fed Victorian London - the elevated iron walkways crossing the street once moved goods between buildings without disturbing traffic below. Derelict by the 1970s, restored by Terence Conran in the 1980s; the walkways are now balconies, but the cobbled Victorian streetscape is intact.
spots.opNote: A public street, walkable any time, best in late afternoon light. A few minutes from Tower Bridge.

spots.name: Sigmund Freud's Final Home
spots.subject: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), founder of psychoanalysis
spots.whyGo: Freud fled Vienna for this house in 1938 and lived here until his death the following year - now the Freud Museum, with his original consulting couch preserved inside.
spots.opNote: The Freud Museum is a paid museum with set opening hours, not just a street plaque.

spots.name: Sir John Gielgud's Westminster Home
spots.subject: Sir John Gielgud (1904–2000), actor
spots.whyGo: One of the defining Shakespearean actors of the 20th century, later known to a much younger audience for Arthur - a plaque a short walk from Westminster Abbey.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Sir Nigel Gresley's Plaque, King's Cross Station
spots.subject: Sir Nigel Gresley (1876–1941), railway locomotive engineer
spots.address: Platform 8, King's Cross Station, Euston Road
spots.whyGo: Gresley designed the Flying Scotsman and the world-speed-record-holding Mallard - the plaque is on Platform 8, the platform his locomotives ran from.
spots.opNote: Inside the station on the platform itself - accessible without a ticket during station opening hours.

spots.name: St Alphage Ruins & Salters' Garden
spots.subject: Medieval church ruins and a fragment of the Roman city wall, wedged between Barbican towers
spots.whyGo: A tiny public garden holds the ruins of St Alphage London Wall church alongside a real stretch of the Roman and medieval city wall, crenellated in 1477 - genuinely ancient London hiding in the concrete geometry of the Barbican.
spots.opNote: Free, always open, easy to walk straight past - it's set back from London Wall itself, reached via Fore Street.

spots.name: Sylvia Pankhurst's Chelsea Home
spots.subject: Sylvia Pankhurst (1882–1960), suffragette and campaigner
spots.whyGo: Pankhurst's plaque sits on the same riverside street as George Eliot's - two very different kinds of significance a few doors apart.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Sylvia Plath's Primrose Hill Home
spots.subject: Sylvia Plath (1932–1963), poet
spots.whyGo: Plath and Ted Hughes lived here early in their marriage - one of the more poignant plaques on the map, a short walk from Primrose Hill itself.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: T.S. Eliot's Kensington Home
spots.subject: T.S. Eliot (1888–1965), poet
spots.whyGo: Eliot lived here in his later years, having already written The Waste Land and Four Quartets - one of Kensington's several literary plaques.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Temple of Mithras (London Mithraeum)
spots.subject: A Roman temple, discovered in 1954, now beneath Bloomberg's HQ
spots.whyGo: Roman Londoners worshipped Mithras here around 240 AD; the ruins were rediscovered during 1954 building work and drew such crowds that the Prime Minister had to weigh in. Now sunk seven metres below Bloomberg's building, with a free reconstruction of temple worship - dimmed lights, chanting, atmospheric smoke.
spots.opNote: Free, but timed-entry tickets must be booked online in advance - it sells out, especially weekends. Closed Sundays and Mondays.

spots.name: The Pankhursts' Notting Hill Home
spots.subject: Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst, suffragette leaders
spots.whyGo: A mother-and-daughter plaque for two of the central figures of the British suffragette movement, on a residential street off Holland Park Avenue.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Trafalgar Square's "Smallest Police Station"
spots.subject: A hollowed-out lamppost built as a covert police observation post in 1926
spots.whyGo: Tucked into the square's southeast corner, this booth was built in 1926 from a hollowed-out ornamental lamppost so up to two officers could quietly watch the square during demonstrations. It's often billed as "Britain's smallest police station", though it never technically had that status.
spots.opNote: Free, visible from the street, easy to miss entirely if you don't know to look for it - it looks like a lamppost.

spots.name: Trinity Buoy Wharf
spots.subject: London's only lighthouse, a shipping-container art village, and a Victorian steamship museum
spots.whyGo: A genuinely odd little peninsula at the mouth of the Lea: London's only lighthouse (used to test navigation lights, not to guide ships), a village of creative studios built from shipping containers, and the SS Robin, a preserved 1890 steamship.
spots.opNote: Free to walk around; the lighthouse's Longplayer sound installation is open weekend afternoons. A fair walk or a short bus ride from Canary Wharf itself - not directly on the Jubilee line.

spots.name: Virginia and Leonard Woolf's Richmond Home
spots.subject: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) and Leonard Woolf, at Hogarth House
spots.whyGo: The Woolfs lived here 1915-1924 and founded the Hogarth Press on the premises, printing early editions of Woolf's own novels and T.S. Eliot's poetry on a hand press in the house.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only. See also the earlier Woolf plaque in Fitzrovia.

spots.name: Virginia Woolf's Fitzroy Square Home
spots.subject: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941), writer, publisher and literary critic
spots.whyGo: Woolf lived here 1907-1911, in the Bloomsbury Group's earliest years before the name Bloomsbury attached itself to the circle. She has a second plaque in Richmond from her later years.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only. See also the Richmond plaque at Hogarth House.

spots.name: Where Keith Moon Played
spots.subject: Keith Moon (1946–1978), drummer, The Who
spots.whyGo: Marks where The Who played in the earliest days of the band, rather than a home address - a different kind of plaque story from the usual "lived here".
spots.opNote: On the former Marquee Club site, now a different business - the plaque is the only trace of the venue at street level.

spots.name: Where Television Was Born
spots.subject: John Logie Baird (1888–1946), television pioneer
spots.whyGo: Baird gave the first public demonstration of television in an attic room here in 1926 - a genuinely world-changing moment on an ordinary Soho street.
spots.opNote: The building is now Bar Italia at street level; the plaque is above.

spots.name: Wilkie Collins's Home
spots.subject: Wilkie Collins (1824–1889), novelist
spots.whyGo: Collins wrote here as one of the pioneers of the detective novel - The Moonstone and The Woman in White both date from his years on this street.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: William Morris's Red Lion Square Home
spots.subject: William Morris (1834–1896), designer and decorative artist
spots.whyGo: Morris founded his decorative arts firm from this address in 1861, before the patterns that now cover half of Britain's National Trust properties existed.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Winston Churchill's Last Home
spots.subject: Winston Churchill (1874–1965), Prime Minister
spots.whyGo: Churchill's home for the last years of his life, a short walk from the Kensington museums.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Ye Olde Mitre
spots.subject: A pub built in 1546 down an alley with no street sign
spots.whyGo: Founded in 1546 for the Bishop of Ely's household staff, tucked down a narrow passage off Hatton Garden with nothing marking the entrance - most people who work nearby never find it. A preserved cherry tree trunk inside is said to mark where Elizabeth I danced with Sir Christopher Hatton.
spots.opNote: No sign on the street - look for the narrow gap between the buildings on Hatton Garden opposite number 8. Two tiny wood-panelled rooms, low ceilings, gets busy after work.
